title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
decision: Adopted a full-system design approach: POWER4 was treated not merely as a chip but as an architecture in which a set of chips (processor, memory and I/O bridge chips) are designed together to realize a system, optimized for SMP operation.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected optimizing the processor chip in isolation. The paper states 'we designed the entire system together, from the processor to memory and I/O bridge chips.'
rationale: A new high-performance processor needs a new subsystem to feed it effectively; system balance must be preserved as technology improvements become available. The team started with the full design in mind up front, marrying process technology, packaging, and microarchitecture so software could exploit them.
outcome: Resulted in a coherent family of parts that together form POWER4 systems scalable up to a 32-way SMP, with the distributed switch interconnect newly introduced to the industry.
weakest_point: Exact phrasing of 'full-system design approach' as a guiding principle heading is from the paper's section 2, but my summary condenses several sentences; the core direction is definitely correct.

title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
decision: Planned from the outset to deliver best-of-breed operating frequencies — embracing the 'speed-demon' approach in addition to IBM's traditional 'brainiac' (complex-design/high-IPC) camp.
alternatives_or_rejected: Prior IBM Unix-based systems had traditionally been in the 'brainiac' camp (more complex design, higher IPC). With POWER4, IBM opted to also embrace the 'speed-demon' approach (high clock rate), rather than continuing with the brainiac-only philosophy.
rationale: To maintain a leadership position, the team planned from the outset to deliver best-of-breed operating frequencies. They revamped chip design with new transistor-level tools and transformed complex control logic into regular dataflow constructs. The system was designed to preserve system balance as technology improvements allow even higher processor frequencies to be delivered.
outcome: POWER4 achieved 1.1–1.3 GHz at launch (industry record for its time), with a design structured to scale to higher frequencies over subsequent process generations.
weakest_point: The 'speed-demon vs brainiac' framing is explicitly stated in IBM's own historical summary of this paper; the paper's Guiding Principles section states the high-frequency intent but may not use those exact labels. Direction is certainly correct.
provenance_note: The 'speed-demon vs brainiac' terminology is quoted from IBM's official history page summarizing this paper; the paper itself uses 'very-high-frequency design' as the principle.

title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
decision: Integrated two processor cores on a single die sharing a unified on-chip L2 cache (split into three autonomous controllers, each feeding 32 bytes/cycle), interconnected via a CIU crossbar — a chip-multiprocessing (CMP) organization.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected building a single wider/complex uniprocessor or two loosely-coupled processors on separate dies. The two processors on the chip share the unified L2 through the CIU, presenting a two-way SMP model to software.
rationale: SMP optimization demanded that a large number of transistors be used to improve total system performance. By placing two cores with a shared unified L2 on one die and connecting them through a CIU crossbar, the design maximized throughput for multi-tasking server environments where multiple processes are active concurrently. Each L2 controller operates concurrently, feeding 32 bytes per cycle to either core's I-cache or D-cache.
outcome: Each POWER4 chip contains 174 million transistors; the two cores share the unified L2 via the CIU crossbar, realizing a two-way SMP on a single die. This became IBM's first multi-core processor.
weakest_point: The transistor count (174M) is from the companion circuit-design paper (Warnock et al.), not exclusively from this system microarchitecture paper; the CMP organization and CIU details are firmly from this paper.
provenance_note: 174M transistor figure is from the companion POWER4 circuit paper, but the dual-core + shared L2 + CIU organization is described in this paper.

title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
decision: Built SMP systems by interconnecting POWER4 chips using a distributed switch topology — four chips per module form an 8-way SMP, and four modules interconnect to form a 32-way SMP, using point-to-point buses rather than a centralized switch.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected conventional centralized-switch or shared-bus SMP interconnects. The paper states the distributed switch interconnect topology 'is new to the industry.'
rationale: To scale to 32-way SMP while preserving bandwidth and low latency, the design uses logically four 16-byte buses between chips on the same module (physically implemented as six unidirectional buses), and two 8-byte buses between modules. The fabric logically appears as a simple low-latency bus to each processor while providing high bandwidth. The eight-way MCM is the building block for the system.
outcome: Enabled 8-way SMP within a multi-chip module and 32-way SMP across four modules; the distributed switch delivered the bandwidth and concurrency needed for commercial and HPC workloads.
weakest_point: The 6-unidirectional-bus implementation detail (3 on, 3 off) is from the paper's Figure 1 description; the high-level distributed-switch decision is unambiguously from the paper.

title: POWER4 system microarchitecture
decision: Adopted an aggressive RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability) philosophy: rather than relying primarily on reliable parts and ECC, the design eliminates outages and provides redundancy where errors cannot be eliminated, transforming hard machine stops (checkstops) into synchronous machine interrupts to software where possible.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected the approach of achieving high reliability solely by 'choosing reliable parts and incorporating ECC logic into major arrays.' The paper explicitly states this approach was insufficient.
rationale: Servers had evolved toward continuous operation. The team required an approach that eliminated outages and provided redundancy in cases where errors could not be eliminated. Where possible, if an error occurred, they transformed hard machine stops into synchronous machine interrupts to software, allowing the system to circumvent problems if possible. RAS was designed to be pervasive throughout the system.
outcome: RAS features became 'as much a part of the design as is anything else'; the design permitted the system to continue operating by handling errors via software-interceptible interrupts rather than hard stops. A more complete discussion is deferred to a companion paper (Bossen et al.).
weakest_point: The defer-to-companion-paper nuance is correctly reflected; the exact wording of 'transforming hard machine stops into synchronous machine interrupts' is from the paper but I'm paraphrasing slightly. Direction and intent are definitely correct.
